A nodemailer Transport, and Mailpit →

What SMTP Actually Does

Sending mail and reading mail are two different protocols — nodemailer, and this project, only ever need the one that sends.

"Email" is really two separate jobs, handled by two separate protocols, and it's easy to blur them together: SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer Protocol) is how a message gets sent — handed from whoever's sending it to a mail server, and from mail server to mail server, until it reaches wherever it's going. POP3 and IMAP are how a message gets read back out of a mailbox afterwards — what an email client like Outlook or Gmail's own app speaks to show you what's sitting in an inbox. Sending a message and later retrieving one are opposite directions over the same underlying system, and each direction has its own protocol because the two jobs need to solve different problems: SMTP cares about routing a message toward a mailbox, IMAP/POP3 about listing and fetching what's already in one.

That split matters here because this project only ever needs one of the two. Nothing in this codebase is a mail client reading an inbox — there's no feature where the API logs into a mailbox and lists messages. Every use of email in this lesson is the API acting purely as a sender: hand a finished message to an SMTP server and be done with it. That's the entire job nodemailer (next slide) does, and the entire job Mailpit needs to fake convincingly for local development — a real SMTP conversation on one end, with no need to also implement IMAP or POP3 as if this were a real mailbox, because nothing is ever going to try to read this project's "sent" folder through them.
